scenario: AITA in relation to my GF's attempt to lose weight? | I've been dating my GF for 3 years. She's upset at her current weight. She's put on about 100lbs since we started dating. I've never mentioned it because she has bipolar disorder, and as I struggle with depression I fully understand how food can take the edge off when you get seriously overwhelmed with depression. But for health reasons and of course other reasons, of course I would like for her to get back to a healthy weight. My girlfriend's bipolar disorder has been a challenge for me, as where I would normally be assertive in a relationship on issues - I often have to back down in arguments because she responds poorly to being challenged. I often feel like I'm walking on ice, but I do my best to try understand her and work at helping her and supporting her as best I can. She is not happy with her current weight, and constantly remarks about it and has been complaining about it for over a year without doing anything about it. I tell her we can work on it together as a team, and both fix our diet. I feel this is the best way to go about it, rather than telling her that SHE needs to lose weight. I don't want her feeling like I'm initiating it, or that it's a journey she needs to take alone. Or that I'm pushing her to do it. For it to be a healthy journey, it needs to be something she is motivated to do and if I do it with her, then it doesn't feel like it's all on her. So, last week she decided to work on her diet. She was upset today because she hasn't lost any weight yet. I told her to not worry about the short term results - that it had only been a week, but to focus on months down the line to see changes. She was extremely defeatist and said she'll never lose weight. This kinda irritated me, because it had only been a week since she started. I felt like she hadn't fully committed, because she was drinking soft drinks and eating chips which are high in carbs so I brought that up, if she wants to see results quicker - that cutting out the junk food completely (rather than cutting down) will help her. Now I understand she's trying to make a change, but the defeatist attitude after only a week is difficult to work with. She then got angry at me and told me to "stop arguing with me about my weight". To which I replied that I wasn't, I had never in our entire relationship brought up her weight, and was just discussing her diet and how she was eating and drinking things that will make her progress slower. She then told me to drop it and leave it alone, and is now in a huff with me for the past few hours over it. I understand this is the nature of her bipolar disorder, and she will shut down anything she's challenged about something. Am I the asshole for challenging her defeatist attitude on her results, when she was taking short-cuts with junk food?

message.reasoning: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out whether I'm "the asshole" in this situation with my girlfriend. Let me start by understanding the scenario. We've been dating for three years, and she's been struggling with her weight, gaining about 100 pounds since we started dating. I know she has bipolar disorder, and I struggle with depression myself, so I understand how food can be a coping mechanism when you're overwhelmed. I've never mentioned her weight directly because of her mental health struggles, but I do want her to get back to a healthy weight for her health and other reasons. She's unhappy with her weight and has been complaining about it for over a year without taking action. I suggested that we work on our diet together as a team, thinking that would make it a more positive and less lonely journey for her. I didn't want her to feel like I was initiating it or that it was something she had to do alone. I wanted it to be a team effort so she wouldn't feel the full pressure of it. Last week, she decided to work on her diet. But today, she was upset because she hasn't lost any weight yet. I tried to reassure her that it's only been a week and to focus on the long-term changes, but she was extremely defeatist, saying she'll never lose weight. This irritated me because it had only been a week since she started. I felt like she hadn't fully committed because she was still drinking soft drinks and eating chips, which are high in carbs. I brought that up, suggesting that if she wants to see quicker results, she should cut out junk food completely rather than just cutting down. I understand she's trying to make a change, but the defeatist attitude after only a week is difficult to work with. She then got angry at me and told me to "stop arguing with me about my weight." I replied that I wasn't bringing up her weight and that I was just discussing her diet and how she was eating and drinking things that would make her progress slower. She then told me to drop it and leave it alone and is now in a huff with me for the past few hours over it. I understand this is the nature of her bipolar disorder, and she will shutdown anything she's challenged about. So, am I "the asshole" for challenging her defeatist attitude on her results when she was taking shortcuts with junk food? First, I need to consider the dynamics of our relationship. She has bipolar disorder, which can make her sensitive to criticism or challenges. I know she's been struggling with her weight and mental health, and I don't want to make things worse by pushing her too hard. On the other hand, I care about her health and want to support her in making positive changes. I suggested working on our diet together as a team, which seems like a good approach because it distributes the responsibility and makes it a shared effort. However, when she started her diet and became upset after only a week without seeing results, I tried to encourage her by focusing on the long-term changes. But she became defeatist, which frustrated me because I felt she wasn't fully committed, especially since she was still eating junk food. I brought up the issue of junk food, suggesting that cutting it out completely could help her see quicker results. But she got angry, feeling like I was arguing with her about her weight. I tried to clarify that I was only discussing her diet and how certain choices were slowing her progress, but she still shut down and became upset. So, is it fair for me to challenge her defeatist attitude and point out that her choices are hindering her progress? Or am I overstepping by trying to push her to make bigger changes, especially considering her mental health struggles? I need to think about the balance between supporting her and encouraging her to make healthier choices without overwhelming her or triggering her bipolar disorder. It's important to be understanding and patient, but it's also reasonable to want her to take responsibility for her health. Maybe I should have approached the conversation differently, focusing more on her feelings and why she's feeling defeated, rather than immediately pointing out what she's doing wrong. That way, I could have shown more empathy and understanding, which might have made her more receptive to discussing her diet and the changes she wants to make. In the future, it might be helpful to have open and non-confrontational conversations about her goals and how we can support each other without making her feel criticized or judged. It's a delicate balance, but being mindful of her mental health and how she responds to challenges is crucial in maintaining a healthy and supportive relationship.
